newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZIER sees NZ economic upturn on tax cut in 1998.
newsitem.headline: NZIER sees NZ economic upturn on tax cut in 1998.

text.p: Despite recent mixed signals the New Zealand economy is close to a turning point and should begin to pick up late in 1997, the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) said in its June quarterly predictions report released on Monday.
The independent research institute forecast annual GDP growth to recover from 2.1 percent in the 1996/97 year to 2.5 percent in 1997/98 before peaking at 4.3 percent in 1998/99.

NZIER said this growth was underpinned by the planned tax cuts in 1998, but could be threatened by diversion into a planned compulsory superannuation scheme which is the subject of a referendum in September this year.
"The most significant risk to these forecasts is that the tax cut will be channelled into a compulsory savings scheme. This would lower forecast growth in 1998/99," NZIER said.
The forecasts were prepared before Treasurer Winston Peters said late last week that government budget surplus forecasts would be lower than some recent private sector forecasts.
Other recent indications of a further slowing in the economy had been had lower than forecast inflation, weak retail sales, declining employment and rising unemployment.
Against this trend, GDP figures released for the December quarter showed the economy growing at more than 2 percent, and export volumes rising despite the high New Zealand dollar.
"Taken together these indicators give a mixed message. Mixed messages usually mean things are starting to change," it said.
The NZIER report noted that even if the economy had not yet passed the turning point it should begin to pick up in late 1997.

This was because economic growth remained robust in most of New Zealand's main trading partners, the exchange rate had stopped its rapid rise and interest rates had eased from their highs of last year.
Adding to growth scenario would be higher government spending, the report went on.
The government will spend about $1 billion more in 1997/98 than was intended prior to the coalition agreement.
But NZIER noted that its forecasts were based on the assumption that New Zealanders would vote no to compulsory super and spend the bulk of their tax cuts.
If the vote was yes, tax cuts would be channelled into savings funds and would lower forecast growth for the 1998/99 year.
The report said superannuation policy would have a big impact on the Government's fiscal position.
"If we stick with the (super) accord we will have to pay higher taxes in the future, but switching to compulsory superannuation will not solve our fiscal problems. It will even bring them forward."
This would happen, the report said, because in the medium term the government would be paying similar superannuation benefits out of a smaller tax take.
The NZIER also forecast underlying inflation to fall to 1.5 percent in the June quarter and hit a low of 0.9 percent in the December 1997 quarter.
Government spending and tax cuts will then push inflation to a peak of 2.4 percent in the September 1999 quarter, but it will be kept under the 3.0 percent upper target by tighter monetary policy.
